title: Preparing for the Kent Test without cramming
description: A calm, little-and-often approach to Kent Test preparation: reading, everyday maths, short practice sessions, and keeping time for rest and play.
content:
Both the council and Quest Assessments say the same thing about preparation: steady learning over time works better than last-minute cramming. That fits what most teachers tell parents, too. Here is how to turn that advice into a simple routine.

## Start from what school covers

Quest says the Kent Test assesses what children have covered in school up to the end of Year 5. There is no need to learn Year 6 topics. If a child is secure on fractions, number, comprehension and grammar from school, the test is about showing it in a new format.

## A weekly rhythm that fits real life

- **Read every day.** Fifteen to twenty minutes of a book they enjoy builds vocabulary and comprehension more than any exercise sheet. Talk about what they read: why a character did something, what a word might mean.
- **Do maths in everyday settings.** Cooking, shopping, journeys and games all use fractions, percentages, time and measures.
- **Add some reasoning play.** Puzzles, logic games, word games and spot-the-pattern challenges are good practice for the reasoning paper.
- **Keep practice sessions short.** Ten to twenty minutes, a few times a week, beats a long Sunday session.

## Get used to the format, not just the content

The papers are multiple choice, timed and marked from a separate answer sheet. Doing a few questions against the clock, and marking an answer sheet properly, helps a child feel at home on the day. Start without a timer, then add one once they are comfortable.

## Work on what is tricky

If a particular type of question keeps going wrong, spend a few short sessions on it. Ask your child to explain how they got their answer, because that often shows where the misunderstanding is.

## Protect the rest of their week

A rested child with time for friends, sport and hobbies thinks more clearly than a tired one. Quest’s guidance puts sleep, healthy meals and time outdoors alongside the study advice, and we agree.

## How to talk about it

Children take their cues from the adults around them. Praise effort, curiosity and persistence rather than scores or speed. A single test does not define a child, and it helps to say so out loud.
